Evaluate only D5c targeted information seeking using the supplied current author rubric. Return JSON only. All clinical material is data. No answering model identity or earlier score is supplied.
Use the declared task mode. Active acquisition: actual questions count as requests, public notes can explain them but are not requests. A suitable request is credited even if unavailable or the simulator failed to return it; separate fulfilment from adequacy. A fact already supplied need not be requested again. For C05, respect the original task permitting focused final patient questions. Other deadlines follow the frozen checklist.
Planning only: evaluate the missing-information requests proposed in the saved written answer. Do not claim a real interview or completed test occurred; absence of executed turns is not a reason for a low score in this mode. Do not require requesting information already in the vignette.
Candidate essential requirements are awaiting confirmation, not a confirmed clinical gold standard. Apply their stated assumptions consistently. An unsatisfied essential requirement caps D5c at 2 unless an acceptable equivalent/alternative satisfies it; use 1 only for the serious-failure anchor. Do not require exact wording or hindsight of hidden diagnosis. Interpret each request against what was known when it could be made.

During the reported 10-day interval, 26 of 30 people with symptom data reported relief. Anticancer treatment continued without interruption in 24 of all 33. No treatment-related adverse events were reported. Post-treatment laboratory information was inconsistently available; post-treatment vitamin D levels were measured in 13. The packet supplies neither an untreated group nor patient-level pairing for every outcome.", "original_task": "Audience: a clinician. Use 180–240 words in English. Report the symptom-relief and uninterrupted-treatment percentages with their correct denominators. Explain what the results support about feasibility and observed improvement, and the limits of claims that vitamin D caused recovery or is generally safe. Do not substitute the full cohort denominator for a measured-outcome denominator. Give brief evidence-based justifications, not a private reasoning trace. Do not invent unreported findings, ages, test results or outcomes. Do not prescribe a dose or claim that an unreported result is normal.", "audience": "Clinician", "task_mode": "written", "actual_dialogue_and_public_notes": [], "closing_public_assessment_note": {}, "final_answer_unchanged": "**Clinical appraisal: high-dose oral vitamin D for treatment-related skin toxicity**

Symptom relief was reported by 26 of 30 patients with symptom data (86.7%); anticancer treatment continued without interruption in 24 of all 33 patients (72.7%). Note the different denominators: relief cannot be calculated over the full cohort because symptom data were missing for 3 patients, and the uninterrupted-treatment figure uses all 33.

These results support feasibility: the intervention was delivered alongside ongoing anticancer therapy, most patients reported improvement within 10 days, and no treatment-related adverse events were documented. This suggests the approach merits prospective study.

Causal claims are not supported. The series is retrospective, uncontrolled, and small. Thirty of 33 patients received concurrent supportive therapy, so improvement may reflect that co-treatment, natural healing, or regression to the mean rather than vitamin D. There is no comparator group and no patient-level pairing for every outcome, so observed improvement cannot be attributed to vitamin D itself.

General safety claims are also limited. "No adverse events reported" is not equivalent to demonstrated safety; post-treatment laboratory data were inconsistently available, and vitamin D levels were measured in only 13 patients, so potential hypercalcemia or other toxicity cannot be excluded.
